metadata.title: Concurrent Computing Knowledge Graph
metadata.description: A detailed, connected machine-readable knowledge graph of concurrent computing: conceptual foundations, execution units, synchronization, hazards, formal models, memory consistency, communication patterns, distributed systems, languages, runtimes, libraries, history, and application domains.

source_basis.uploaded_source: Concurrent computing article text supplied by the user
source_coverage: definition and distinction from parallel computing
shared resources, race conditions, deadlocks and starvation
source_basis.expansion_note: The uploaded source's terminology and language list are expanded with general computer-science knowledge to create a connected graph. Historical/current status and language-version specifics may vary.

id_conventions.relationship_ids: rel_ followed by a zero-padded sequence number
id_conventions.relationship_direction: source to target; direction reflects the described semantic relation

coverage: processes, threads, coroutines, tasks and scheduling
shared memory, message passing and synchronization
races, deadlock, livelock, starvation and performance hazards
atomic operations, lock-free algorithms and memory models
actors, CSP, process calculi, Petri nets, dataflow and tuple spaces
formal specification, temporal logic, model checking and testing
async I/O, futures, promises, channels, structured concurrency and backpressure
distributed systems, transactions, consensus and consistency
libraries, runtimes, APIs, hardware, operating systems and application domains
history, researchers and classic synchronization problems

entities.name: Concurrent computing
entities.description: A system or program is concurrent when multiple computations can make progress during overlapping lifetimes; their steps may interleave on one processor or execute simultaneously on several processors or machines.

entities.name: Concurrency
entities.description: The property that multiple activities are in progress during overlapping periods, without requiring simultaneous physical execution.

entities.name: Parallel computing
entities.description: Execution of computational work simultaneously on multiple processing units, commonly to reduce elapsed time or increase throughput.

entities.name: Sequential computing
entities.description: A computation proceeds in a single ordered chain in which each step follows the preceding step.

entities.name: Serial schedule
entities.description: A schedule that executes tasks one at a time without interleaving their operations.

entities.name: Interleaving
entities.description: A scheduler alternates steps from different activities, creating overlapping lifetimes even when only one activity executes at a particular instant.

entities.name: Scheduler
entities.description: The component that chooses which runnable task, thread, process, or actor receives execution time.

entities.name: Task
entities.description: A unit of work that can be scheduled, suspended, resumed, completed, cancelled, or failed.

entities.name: Process
entities.description: An operating-system execution environment with its own address space and resources.

entities.name: Thread
entities.description: An execution path within a process; threads usually share the process address space and can access common mutable state.

entities.name: Coroutine
entities.description: A resumable computation that can suspend and later continue, often cooperatively and with lower overhead than an OS thread.

entities.name: Fiber
entities.description: A lightweight user-space execution unit scheduled by a runtime or library.

entities.name: Event loop
entities.description: A loop that dispatches callbacks and resumes asynchronous operations as events or completions arrive.

entities.name: Asynchronous programming
entities.description: A style in which an operation can start and return control before completion; completion is represented by callbacks, futures, promises, events, or awaited results.

entities.name: Concurrency versus parallelism
entities.description: Concurrency concerns overlapping progress and structuring interactions; parallelism concerns simultaneous execution. A system can have either, both, or neither.

entities.name: Distributed computing
entities.description: Computations run across networked machines whose components communicate over message passing and must handle partial failures and uncertain timing.

entities.name: Shared-memory model
entities.description: Concurrent components communicate through memory locations visible to more than one execution unit.

entities.name: Message-passing model
entities.description: Concurrent components exchange explicit messages rather than directly manipulating each other's local state.

entities.name: Concurrency control
entities.description: Mechanisms and protocols that coordinate concurrent operations to preserve invariants, ordering, and data integrity.

entities.name: Synchronization
entities.description: Coordination of execution timing or ordering so operations occur under required conditions.

entities.name: Communication
entities.description: The transfer of data or events between concurrent components, either implicitly or explicitly.

entities.name: Resource sharing
entities.description: Multiple activities access a common resource such as memory, files, sockets, devices, database records, or service capacity.

entities.name: Throughput
entities.description: Amount of useful work completed per unit time.

entities.name: Latency
entities.description: Elapsed time from an operation being requested to its completion or response.

entities.name: Responsiveness
entities.description: The ability of a system to remain interactive and promptly react while other work waits or runs.

entities.name: Scalability
entities.description: The ability to maintain useful performance as workload, users, data, or available resources increase.

entities.name: Nondeterminism
entities.description: The same program and input may produce different valid outcomes because scheduling and message arrival order vary.

entities.name: Execution trace
entities.description: An ordered record of events or actions in one possible execution of a concurrent system.

entities.name: Happens-before relation
entities.description: A partial order capturing causal ordering between events, introduced by program order and synchronization or message communication.

entities.name: Linearizability
entities.description: A concurrent operation appears to take effect atomically at some point between invocation and response while respecting real-time order.

entities.name: Serializability
entities.description: A concurrent transaction schedule is equivalent in effect to some serial ordering of those transactions.

entities.name: Sequential consistency
entities.description: A result is equivalent to some single global ordering of operations that preserves each processor's program order.

entities.name: Memory model
entities.description: Rules specifying which memory reads and writes are visible to which threads and which reorderings are allowed.

entities.name: Atomicity
entities.description: An operation is observed as indivisible with respect to competing operations.

entities.name: Memory visibility
entities.description: Whether writes made by one execution unit become observable by another under the memory model.

entities.name: Memory ordering
entities.description: Constraints on the order in which memory operations may become observable.

entities.name: Mutual exclusion
entities.description: At most one execution unit at a time may enter a protected critical section for a given lock or resource.

entities.name: Critical section
entities.description: A region that accesses shared state and must obey an exclusion or synchronization protocol.

entities.name: Shared-state invariant
entities.description: A condition over shared data that must remain true across every externally observable state transition.

entities.name: Backpressure
entities.description: A producer is slowed, blocked, or told to reduce production when downstream capacity is insufficient.

entities.name: Cancellation
entities.description: A request to stop work, requiring defined propagation, cleanup, and handling of cancellation points.

entities.name: Structured concurrency
entities.description: A discipline in which concurrent tasks are scoped to a parent operation, with explicit lifetime, cancellation, and error propagation.

entities.name: Resource lifetime management
entities.description: Rules that determine when tasks, handles, locks, sockets, and other resources are created, transferred, and released.

entities.name: Race condition
entities.description: Behavior depends on an uncontrolled timing or ordering of concurrent operations.

entities.name: Data race
entities.description: Two threads access the same memory location concurrently, at least one access writes, and no required synchronization orders them; language-specific consequences may include undefined behavior.

entities.name: Deadlock
entities.description: Two or more activities wait indefinitely for resources or events that only the waiting activities can provide.

entities.name: Livelock
entities.description: Activities continue changing state or retrying but make no useful forward progress.

entities.name: Starvation
entities.description: An activity is indefinitely denied a resource or execution opportunity while others continue progressing.

entities.name: Priority inversion
entities.description: A high-priority task is blocked by a lower-priority task holding a needed resource, potentially worsened by medium-priority work.

entities.name: Lost wakeup
entities.description: A notification occurs between a condition check and wait registration, causing a waiter to sleep despite the condition being true.

entities.name: False sharing
entities.description: Independent variables on the same cache line cause cache-coherence traffic when different cores modify them.

entities.name: Contention
entities.description: Multiple execution units compete for the same lock, cache line, queue, CPU, or other limited resource.

entities.name: Resource starvation
entities.description: A resource remains unavailable to an activity because competing work repeatedly obtains it first.

entities.name: Liveness
entities.description: A property that required progress eventually occurs, such as a request eventually completing.

entities.name: Safety
entities.description: A property that bad states never occur, such as two threads never simultaneously owning an exclusive lock.

entities.name: Mutex
entities.description: A mutual-exclusion lock protecting a critical section or shared invariant.

entities.name: Semaphore
entities.description: A counter-based synchronization primitive used to control access to a limited number of resources or signal events.

entities.name: Counting semaphore
entities.description: A semaphore whose counter represents the number of available permits or resources.

entities.name: Binary semaphore
entities.description: A semaphore constrained to a binary permit state, often used for signaling or simple exclusion.

entities.name: Monitor
entities.description: A construct that encapsulates shared state and operations with implicit mutual exclusion and condition synchronization.

entities.name: Condition variable
entities.description: A primitive allowing threads to sleep until notified, normally used with a mutex and a predicate checked in a loop.

entities.name: Read-write lock
entities.description: A lock that permits multiple readers or one writer, subject to fairness and upgrade rules.

entities.name: Spinlock
entities.description: A lock in which a contender repeatedly checks availability instead of sleeping; useful only in constrained short-wait contexts.

entities.name: Barrier
entities.description: A rendezvous point that prevents participating tasks from proceeding until the required participants arrive.

entities.name: Latch
entities.description: A one-shot synchronization gate that opens when a specified count reaches zero.

entities.name: Atomic operation
entities.description: An indivisible operation on shared state, often provided by hardware instructions and language libraries.

entities.name: Compare-and-swap
entities.description: An atomic conditional update that changes a location only if it matches an expected value.

entities.name: Fetch-add
entities.description: An atomic read-modify-write operation that adds a value and returns the prior value.

entities.name: Memory fence
entities.description: An ordering primitive that constrains visibility or reordering of memory operations according to the language memory model.

entities.name: Thread-local storage
entities.description: State with a distinct instance per thread, reducing sharing but requiring lifecycle and propagation awareness.

entities.name: Lock-free algorithm
entities.description: An algorithm guaranteeing system-wide progress: some operation completes in a finite number of steps even if individual operations can starve.

entities.name: Wait-free algorithm
entities.description: An algorithm in which every operation completes in a bounded number of its own steps.

entities.name: Obstruction-free algorithm
entities.description: An algorithm that guarantees progress for an operation running alone for long enough.

entities.name: Lock ordering
entities.description: A consistent global order for acquiring multiple locks to prevent circular-wait deadlocks.

entities.name: Optimistic concurrency control
entities.description: Operations proceed without exclusive locking and validate conflicts before committing or retrying.

entities.name: Pessimistic concurrency control
entities.description: Operations acquire locks or reservations before performing conflict-sensitive work.

entities.name: Software transactional memory
entities.description: Shared-memory updates are grouped into transactions that commit atomically or abort and retry on conflict.

entities.name: Reentrant lock
entities.description: A lock that the owning thread may acquire repeatedly, usually tracking a hold count.

entities.name: Once initialization
entities.description: A facility ensures initialization code runs once safely despite concurrent callers.

entities.name: Actor model
entities.description: A model in which actors encapsulate state and communicate by sending asynchronous messages; actors process messages sequentially and can create actors or change behavior.

entities.name: Communicating Sequential Processes (CSP)
entities.description: A process algebra and programming model describing independent processes that interact through communication channels and synchronization.

entities.name: Process calculus
entities.description: A family of algebraic formalisms for describing concurrent processes and their communication and behavior.

entities.name: Calculus of Communicating Systems (CCS)
entities.description: A process calculus for reasoning algebraically about interacting concurrent processes.

entities.name: Pi-calculus
entities.description: A process calculus that models communication and dynamic changes in connectivity through channel passing.

entities.name: Petri net
entities.description: A graph-based model with places, transitions, and tokens for representing state, synchronization, resource use, and concurrent event firing.

entities.name: Parallel random-access machine (PRAM)
entities.description: An abstract model of parallel processors sharing a common memory, useful for algorithm analysis.

entities.name: Bulk synchronous parallel (BSP)
entities.description: A parallel computation model organized into computation phases separated by global communication or synchronization supersteps.

entities.name: Tuple space
entities.description: An associative shared space in which processes publish and retrieve tuples, enabling decoupled coordination.

entities.name: Linda
entities.description: A coordination language based on tuple-space operations such as output, input, and read.

entities.name: SCOOP
entities.description: Simple Concurrent Object-Oriented Programming, an Eiffel-related model using contracts and controlled access to separate objects.

entities.name: Reo coordination language
entities.description: A channel-based coordination language for composing connectors and specifying communication constraints.

entities.name: Trace monoid
entities.description: A mathematical representation of event sequences modulo equivalence of independent actions.

entities.name: Input/output automata
entities.description: A model of components with input, output, and internal actions, used to specify and verify distributed and concurrent systems.

entities.name: Tagged-signal model
entities.description: A unifying model of computation using events tagged with ordering or timing information to describe different concurrent semantics.

entities.name: Dataflow model
entities.description: Computation is triggered when input data becomes available; dependencies in a graph define the allowed execution order.

entities.name: Flow-based programming
entities.description: Applications are composed from processes that exchange structured data through bounded or unbounded flows.

entities.name: Temporal logic
entities.description: A logic for expressing properties across execution states or action sequences over time.

entities.name: Linear temporal logic (LTL)
entities.description: A temporal logic that expresses properties over individual paths or traces, including eventuality and invariance.

entities.name: Computation tree logic (CTL)
entities.description: A branching-time temporal logic that expresses properties across possible execution paths.

entities.name: TLA+
entities.description: A formal specification language based on temporal logic and set theory, used to model and check concurrent and distributed algorithms.

entities.name: Model checking
entities.description: Automated exploration of a finite or abstract state space to check whether a system satisfies specified properties.

entities.name: Formal verification
entities.description: Mathematical reasoning or automated checking used to establish that an implementation or model satisfies a specification.

entities.name: Concurrency testing
entities.description: Testing strategies that explore scheduling variations, race windows, interleavings, and concurrent histories.

entities.name: Linearizability testing
entities.description: Checking whether observed concurrent operation histories can be explained by a legal sequential history respecting real-time constraints.

entities.name: Future
entities.description: A handle for a result that may become available later; operations can compose, wait for, or transform the eventual result.

entities.name: Promise
entities.description: A write-side object used to complete a future with a value or failure.

entities.name: async/await
entities.description: Syntax that lets asynchronous functions suspend at await points and resume when awaited operations complete.

entities.name: Callback
entities.description: A function registered to be invoked when an event or asynchronous operation completes.

entities.name: Channel
entities.description: A typed or untyped conduit for passing values between concurrent tasks; semantics may be buffered, unbuffered, synchronous, or asynchronous.

entities.name: Rendezvous communication
entities.description: A synchronous exchange in which sender and receiver meet before communication completes.

entities.name: Buffered channel
entities.description: A channel with finite or otherwise defined queue capacity that can decouple producer and consumer timing.

entities.name: Actor mailbox
entities.description: A queue of messages delivered to an actor for sequential processing.

entities.name: Worker pool
entities.description: A fixed or dynamically sized set of workers that pulls tasks from a queue to bound resource usage.

entities.name: Producer-consumer pattern
entities.description: One or more producers generate work that one or more consumers process, commonly connected by a queue or channel.

entities.name: Fork-join
entities.description: A task splits into child tasks and later joins or awaits their completion.

entities.name: MapReduce
entities.description: A model that maps independent inputs to intermediate results and reduces those results into an aggregate.

entities.name: Pipeline concurrency
entities.description: Work is divided into stages that operate concurrently on different items, with flow control between stages.

entities.name: Work stealing
entities.description: Idle workers take tasks from busier workers' queues to balance parallel workloads.

entities.name: Thread pool
entities.description: A reusable set of worker threads that executes submitted tasks while controlling thread creation overhead and concurrency.

entities.name: Thread safety
entities.description: An abstraction remains correct when accessed by multiple threads according to its documented concurrency contract.

entities.name: Reentrancy
entities.description: A routine can be entered again before an earlier invocation completes without corrupting shared state or relying on unsafe hidden state.

entities.name: Actor supervision
entities.description: A parent actor or supervisor monitors child failures and applies restart, stop, resume, or escalation policies.

entities.name: Reactive Streams
entities.description: A protocol for asynchronous stream processing with explicit demand and backpressure.

entities.name: Asynchronous I/O
entities.description: An I/O operation can be initiated without blocking the initiating execution unit until completion.

entities.name: Event-driven architecture
entities.description: Components react to events and communicate through event notifications, queues, or brokers.

entities.name: Distributed consensus
entities.description: Processes agree on a value or ordered log despite message delays and specified failure assumptions.

entities.name: Failure detector
entities.description: A mechanism or abstraction that suspects component failures from timing and communication observations, which may be imperfect in asynchronous systems.

entities.name: Clock synchronization
entities.description: Techniques for aligning or estimating clocks across machines despite drift and network delay.

entities.name: Distributed transaction
entities.description: A transaction spans multiple services, nodes, or resource managers and requires coordination or compensating semantics.

entities.name: Two-phase commit (2PC)
entities.description: A coordinator asks participants to prepare, then commits or aborts; it can block if the coordinator fails in critical states.

entities.name: Eventual consistency
entities.description: Replicas converge if updates stop and communication or repair continues, without promising immediate agreement.

entities.name: Multi-version concurrency control (MVCC)
entities.description: A database technique that retains multiple row or object versions so readers can often proceed without blocking writers.

entities.name: Transaction
entities.description: A group of operations treated as a unit, often specified through atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability.

entities.name: ACID properties
entities.description: Atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability properties commonly used to characterize database transactions.

entities.name: Transaction isolation level
entities.description: A contract describing which anomalies may be observed by concurrent transactions.

entities.name: Distributed lock
entities.description: A coordination mechanism intended to grant exclusive ownership across machines, requiring careful lease, fencing, and failure semantics.

entities.name: Idempotency
entities.description: Repeating an operation has the same intended effect as performing it once, supporting safe retries under uncertainty.

entities.name: At-least-once delivery
entities.description: A delivery guarantee that may duplicate messages and therefore often requires idempotent processing.

entities.name: At-most-once delivery
entities.description: A delivery guarantee that avoids duplicate delivery but may lose messages.

entities.name: Exactly-once processing
entities.description: A system-level claim that effects are applied once within a defined scope; usually requires transactional or deduplication mechanisms rather than a network guarantee alone.

entities.name: Multicore processor
entities.description: A processor package containing multiple cores capable of executing threads in parallel.

entities.name: Symmetric multiprocessing (SMP)
entities.description: A multiprocessor architecture in which processors share main memory and are managed by a common operating system.

entities.name: Cache coherence
entities.description: Hardware mechanisms that maintain a coherent view of cache lines shared among processor cores.

entities.name: Operating-system multitasking
entities.description: The operating system switches among processes or threads, enabling overlapping progress and resource sharing.

entities.name: Preemptive scheduling
entities.description: The scheduler can interrupt a running task to give another task execution time.

entities.name: Cooperative scheduling
entities.description: A running task yields control at defined points rather than being forcibly preempted by the user-space scheduler.

entities.name: Time-sharing
entities.description: Processor time is divided among multiple activities so each can make progress.

entities.name: Interrupt
entities.description: An event that temporarily diverts execution to a handler, enabling prompt response to hardware or software events.

entities.name: Interrupt handler
entities.description: Code executed in response to an interrupt, typically subject to strict constraints on blocking and allowed operations.

entities.name: Real-time concurrency
entities.description: Concurrent execution under timing constraints, where meeting deadlines can be as important as logical correctness.

entities.name: Embedded concurrency
entities.description: Concurrency in resource-constrained devices, often involving interrupts, tasks, peripherals, and real-time scheduling.

entities.name: High-performance computing (HPC)
entities.description: Large-scale computation using parallel and distributed resources, often with explicit communication and synchronization.

entities.name: Web-server concurrency
entities.description: A server handles overlapping client requests using threads, event loops, asynchronous I/O, actors, or worker processes.

entities.name: Database concurrency
entities.description: Database engines coordinate concurrent readers and writers while preserving transaction isolation and consistency.

entities.name: Cloud and service concurrency
entities.description: Services process many overlapping requests and background jobs while controlling resource usage, failures, and backpressure.

entities.name: Network concurrency
entities.description: Independent network endpoints, sessions, and protocols progress concurrently with variable delays and failures.

entities.name: GUI concurrency
entities.description: Applications perform background work while preserving responsive UI updates and respecting UI-thread constraints.

entities.name: Scientific dataflow computing
entities.description: Scientific workloads express dependencies among data-processing stages that can run concurrently when inputs are ready.

entities.name: Financial system concurrency
entities.description: Financial software coordinates concurrent orders, balances, ledgers, and risk checks while maintaining strict invariants.

entities.name: GPU concurrency
entities.description: GPU programs execute many threads or work-items across compute units, with device-specific memory and synchronization models.

entities.name: Distributed system
entities.description: A collection of networked components that coordinate through messages and must account for latency, partial failure, and independent clocks.

entities.name: C
entities.description: C provides concurrency through platform APIs and, since C11, standard threads and atomics where implementations support them.

concurrency_mechanisms: mutexes/condition variables via C11 threads or platform libraries

entities.name: C++
entities.description: C++ supports threads, atomics, mutexes, condition variables, futures, promises, parallel algorithms, and C++20 coroutines.

entities.name: Java
entities.description: Java offers JVM threads, synchronized monitors, volatile visibility, java.util.concurrent locks, executors, futures, completable futures, and structured concurrency APIs in evolving releases.

entities.name: C#
entities.description: C#/.NET supports tasks, async/await, threads, locks, concurrent collections, channels, cancellation tokens, and parallel libraries.

entities.name: Go
entities.description: Go uses goroutines and channels, with select, mutexes, wait groups, contexts, and a runtime scheduler; its design is influenced by CSP.

entities.name: Erlang
entities.description: Erlang is designed for massive lightweight-process concurrency with asynchronous message passing, per-process state, supervision, and fault-tolerant OTP patterns.

entities.name: Elixir
entities.description: Elixir runs on the BEAM VM and uses processes, message passing, tasks, supervisors, and OTP abstractions.

entities.name: Rust
entities.description: Rust supports native threads, channels, async futures, atomics, and ownership/borrowing rules that help prevent data races in safe code.

entities.name: Python
entities.description: Python offers threading, multiprocessing, concurrent.futures, asyncio, queues, and synchronization primitives; parallel CPU execution depends on interpreter/runtime and extension details.

entities.name: JavaScript
entities.description: JavaScript commonly uses event-loop concurrency, promises, async/await and callbacks; Web Workers and worker threads provide separate execution contexts where available.

entities.name: TypeScript
entities.description: TypeScript adds static typing to JavaScript and uses JavaScript's event-loop, promise, worker, and asynchronous APIs.

entities.name: Kotlin
entities.description: Kotlin supports JVM threads and executors as well as coroutine-based structured concurrency through kotlinx.coroutines.

entities.name: Scala
entities.description: Scala supports JVM concurrency, Futures, actors through libraries, and effect/stream ecosystems such as Cats Effect, ZIO, and FS2.

entities.name: Haskell
entities.description: Haskell supports lightweight threads, STM, MVars, channels, asynchronous exceptions, and parallel strategies under a pure functional model.

entities.name: OCaml
entities.description: OCaml offers system threads and, in newer versions, domains for parallel execution, plus effects and libraries for asynchronous I/O and concurrency.

entities.name: F#
entities.description: F#/.NET supports async workflows, tasks, agents/mailboxes, parallel collections, and the .NET concurrency libraries.

entities.name: Swift
entities.description: Swift supports async/await, actors, task groups, cancellation, and structured concurrency, with Sendable and isolation rules to reason about data sharing.

entities.name: Dart
entities.description: Dart commonly uses asynchronous futures and streams and isolate-based concurrency with message passing rather than shared mutable memory.

entities.name: Ruby
entities.description: Ruby offers threads, fibers, queues, mutexes, and asynchronous I/O; parallel CPU execution and scheduling behavior depend on implementation/runtime.

entities.name: PHP
entities.description: PHP's typical request model is process-oriented, with optional concurrency approaches through extensions, event loops, and worker systems.

entities.name: Perl
entities.description: Perl supports threads and shared variables through threads/shared modules, plus process-based concurrency and asynchronous libraries.

entities.name: Raku
entities.description: Raku includes threads, promises, supplies, channels, and asynchronous task primitives in its concurrency model.

entities.name: Julia
entities.description: Julia supports tasks, cooperative scheduling, channels, distributed workers, multithreading, and async/wait-style coordination.

entities.name: Fortran
entities.description: Modern Fortran supports coarrays and image-based parallelism, DO CONCURRENT, and interoperability with OpenMP or MPI.

entities.name: Ada
entities.description: Ada has language-defined tasking, protected objects, rendezvous entry calls, and real-time scheduling facilities.

entities.name: D
entities.description: D provides threads, message-passing helpers, fibers, and concurrency libraries, with an actor-oriented ecosystem.

entities.name: Clojure
entities.description: Clojure offers futures, promises, agents, atoms, refs, and software transactional memory on the JVM.

entities.name: E
entities.description: The E language emphasizes object-capability security and promise-based asynchronous message passing to reduce common deadlock patterns.

entities.name: Eiffel
entities.description: Eiffel's SCOOP model coordinates concurrent calls to separate objects and integrates contracts into concurrency reasoning.

entities.name: COBOL
entities.description: COBOL applications commonly use transaction monitors, operating-system tasks, database concurrency, and platform-specific threading rather than one universal language-native model.

entities.name: Lisp and Scheme dialects
entities.description: Lisp-family implementations provide varied concurrency facilities including threads, futures, actors, and parallel extensions; MultiLisp historically explored parallel Scheme.

entities.name: Oz / Mozart
entities.description: Oz is a multiparadigm language with dataflow variables, threads, futures, and message-passing and shared-state mechanisms.

entities.name: LabVIEW
entities.description: LabVIEW's dataflow execution model schedules nodes when their inputs are available and offers explicit parallel loops and synchronization primitives.

entities.name: VHDL
entities.description: VHDL models concurrent hardware processes and signal updates, where concurrent statements describe hardware behavior rather than OS threads.

entities.name: XC
entities.description: XC is a C-derived language for XMOS devices with CSP-inspired channels and explicit parallel constructs for programmable I/O.

entities.name: occam and occam-π
entities.description: occam-family languages express concurrent processes communicating through channels, strongly influenced by CSP; occam-π adds mobile channels and π-calculus ideas.

entities.name: Concurrent Haskell
entities.description: Concurrent Haskell adds concurrency abstractions such as lightweight threads, MVars, channels, and STM to Haskell.

entities.name: Concurrent ML
entities.description: Concurrent ML extends ML with typed synchronous communication channels and first-class communication events.

entities.name: Modula-2 and Modula-3
entities.description: Modula-family languages historically provide coroutine or thread facilities; Modula-3 includes threads, mutexes, and condition variables.

entities.name: Pony
entities.description: Pony is an actor-oriented language designed around reference capabilities and data-race freedom for concurrent actors.

entities.name: ParaSail
entities.description: ParaSail is designed for parallel programming and aims to eliminate common data races through language-level restrictions.

entities.name: X10
entities.description: X10 is a research language designed for concurrency and scalable parallelism using places, activities, and finish/async constructs.

entities.name: Orc
entities.description: Orc is a concurrent orchestration language for composing site calls and coordinating parallel, sequential, and competitive computations.

entities.name: Joule
entities.description: Joule is a dataflow-oriented language in which concurrent components communicate through message passing.

entities.name: JoCaml
entities.description: JoCaml extends OCaml with join-calculus constructs for concurrent and distributed channel-based coordination.

entities.name: Limbo
entities.description: Limbo is a language for the Inferno operating system with channels and concurrent processes, historically related to Alef.

entities.name: Alef
entities.description: Alef was a systems language associated with early Plan 9 that combined threads and message passing.

entities.name: Newsqueak
entities.description: Newsqueak is a research language with first-class channels and concurrent processes, influencing later channel-oriented languages.

entities.name: Axum
